extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, in-house IP counsel, and practitioners evaluating IPR/PGR strategy
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and analysis on when the USPTO Director (and the PTAB) may exercise discretion to deny institution of inter partes reviews (IPRs) and post-grant reviews (PGRs), including procedural changes, enumerated considerations, and how practitioners should adapt petition strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. § 314(a) institution standard
rubrics_metrics.description: 35 U.S.C. § 314(a) provides limits on when the Director is permitted to institute an IPR, requiring the Director to first determine that there is a “reasonable likelihood that the petitioner would prevail with respect to at least 1 of the claims challenged in the petition,” but does not enumerate any circumstances or facts under which the Director is required to institute an IPR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statutory 'reasonable likelihood' threshold governs institution on the merits, but does not deprive the Director of discretion to deny institution for other reasons; petitions must still clear this merits threshold if referred to the Board.

rubrics_metrics.name: Director's discretion over institution (role of Director vs Board)
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically the Director's discretion to deny was delegated to and exercised by the Board; recent memoranda (Boalick Memo, Workload Management Memo) and the October 17, 2025 NPFM centralize discretionary-denial decisionmaking with the Director and require the Director to decide discretionary denial issues before institution on the merits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must now anticipate Director-level review of discretionary factors (and under proposed rules possibly merits issues at institution), rather than relying only on Board practice or prior Board precedential decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fintiv factors
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board articulated a six-factor test to determine “whether efficiency, fairness, and the merits support the exercise of authority to deny institution in view of an earlier trial date in the parallel proceeding.” (Apple v. Fintiv).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fintiv factors have been the most frequent basis for discretionary denial—particularly where a parallel district court trial date is earlier than the projected final written decision date. Under current practice these factors carry renewed weight even when petitioners file stipulations such as Sotera stipulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sotera stipulations (stipulation re not pursuing grounds in district court)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Sotera stipulation is a stipulation in parallel district court litigation stating that “if IPR is instituted, [petitioner] will not pursue in the District Court Litigation any ground raised or that could have been reasonably raised in an IPR.” Sotera rulings and Director Vidal's 2022 memo previously treated such stipulations as dispositive against discretionary denial in view of parallel district court litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post-2025 guidance: Sotera stipulations are still “highly relevant” but “will not be dispositive by itself”; petitioners should not view them as a silver bullet. Failure to file a Sotera stipulation can still be cited against a petition. More protective or broader stipulations (e.g., not raising 102/103 grounds or not relying on the same evidence in any other proceeding) may be required under proposed rules but even expanded stipulations may not overcome strong discretionary concerns like settled expectations or early trial dates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workload Management Memo — procedural bifurcation (DD Request / DD Response)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Workload Management Memo instituted a new process: the patent owner files a separate, standalone brief within two months of the filing date of the petition devoted entirely to discretionary denial issues (the “DD Request”); the petitioner then has one month to submit an opposition brief (the “DD Response”). All discretionary denial issues are decided by the Director before any institution decision; if the Director determines discretionary denial is appropriate, institution is denied before the projected date for an institution decision on the merits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This procedural change requires a new discrete pleading strategy (timely DD Request/Response); petitioners should prepare to address director-level discretionary concerns early and tailor petitions to avoid triggering denial. The shift also means discretionary denials are resolved before the usual merits clock, changing timing and resource expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether the PTAB or another forum has already adjudicated the validity or patentability of the challenged patent claims
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the Workload Management Memo's listed “relevant considerations” is: whether the PTAB or another forum has already adjudicated the validity or patentability of the challenged patent claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If validity has been previously adjudicated (e.g., prior IPR, district court judgment), that fact weighs strongly toward discretionary denial; the NPFM further implements this by specifying that IPRs are unavailable if the challenged patent’s validity was previously upheld in another proceeding (proposed 37 § 42.108(e)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether there have been changes in the law or new judicial precedent since issuance of the claims that may affect patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: The Workload Management Memo lists as a relevant consideration whether there have been changes in the law or new judicial precedent issued since issuance of the claims that may affect patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A change in law or new precedent that undermines the patent owner’s position may favor institution; conversely, settled later precedent that supports patentability may favor denial. Petitioners should highlight favorable intervening precedent and show why review is appropriate despite prior legal developments.

rubrics_metrics.name: The strength of the unpatentability challenge
rubrics_metrics.description: The Workload Management Memo lists the 'strength of the unpatentability challenge' as a relevant consideration for discretionary denial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A persuasive, well-supported merits showing makes institution more likely when discretionary denial is considered; weak or marginal challenges are more vulnerable to denial on discretionary grounds. Emphasize claim charts, clear prior art disclosures, and direct nexus to claim language to demonstrate strength.

rubrics_metrics.name: The extent of the petition’s reliance on expert testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: The Workload Management Memo lists 'the extent of the petition’s reliance on expert testimony' as a relevant consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heavy reliance on expert declarations (rather than intrinsic or publicly available evidence) can be a negative discretionary factor. Petitioners should minimize unnecessary expert dependence in institution-stage showings and emphasize documentary/prior art evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compelling economic, public health, or national security interests
rubrics_metrics.description: The Workload Management Memo lists 'compelling economic, public health, or national security interests' as a relevant consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where strong public-interest considerations exist, the Director may favor institution or denial depending on whether adjudication by the PTAB serves those interests. Parties should frame such considerations clearly when relevant (e.g., explain economic impact or public-health implications).

rubrics_metrics.name: Other considerations bearing on the Director’s discretion (catchall)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Workload Management Memo includes 'any other considerations bearing on the Director’s discretion' as an explicitly enumerated, catchall relevant consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Director retains broad discretion to weigh additional factors not enumerated; parties should identify and brief unique case-specific equities or facts (e.g., investments, licensing history, enforcement behavior) that may affect the discretionary calculus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Settled expectations (length of time claims have been in force) — detailed standard and rebuttals
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'settled expectations' consideration — such as 'the length of time the claims have been in force' — is highlighted as a newly prominent basis for discretionary denial. The Director has said there is 'no bright-line rule' but decisions show a practical pattern: patents >6 years often yield findings of 'strong settled expectations' while patents <6 years often do not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Settled expectations is now one of the predominant bases for discretionary denial. However, it is not dispositive; petitioners can rebut settled-expectations concerns by showing facts like lack of commercialization/assertion/marking/licensing in the petitioner’s technology space, evidence of examiner error or overlooked prior art in prosecution, or patent expiry (which may tilt back toward institution). Practitioners should marshal specific factual evidence to rebut settled expectations when challenging older patents (examples: no prior enforcement against petitioner's industry, unexercised patents, prosecution history showing missed prior art).

rubrics_metrics.name: NPFM: tightened stipulation requirement (Sotera-stipulation replacement)
rubrics_metrics.description: The October 17, 2025 Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPFM) codifies that a Sotera stipulation is no longer sufficient by itself and would require a stipulation that “petitioner will not raise grounds of invalidity or unpatentability with respect to the challenged patent under 35 U.S.C. 102 or 103”—which includes prior art systems—in any other proceeding (Proposed 37 § 42.108(d)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under the proposed rule, petitioners may need broader, more restrictive stipulations to avoid discretionary denial. Even with such stipulations, the Director may still find discretionary denial appropriate based on other considerations (e.g., settled expectations, prior adjudications).

rubrics_metrics.name: NPFM: prior-upheld validity bars IPR (proposed 37 § 42.108(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: The NPFM specifies that IPRs are unavailable if the challenged patent’s validity was previously upheld in another proceeding, including by a district court on summary judgment or in trial, a prior IPR, or a prior ex parte reexamination (Proposed 37 § 42.108(e)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This proposed codification aligns with recent discretionary-denial decisions; where a patent's validity has already been sustained in another forum, petitioners face a strong bar to institution. Parties should evaluate prior final outcomes before filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: NPFM: trial-before-FWD rule (more likely than not a district court or ITC trial before final written decision)
rubrics_metrics.description: The NPFM provides that an IPR will not be instituted if, 'more likely than not,' there will be a district court or ITC trial before the due date of the final written decision in the IPR (Proposed 37 § 42.108(f)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This makes timing of parallel proceedings a dispositive consideration under the proposed rule; practitioners must carefully evaluate time-to-trial versus projected PTAB final written decision dates when deciding whether to file an IPR. Early trial dates in district court or ITC significantly increase the risk of discretionary denial.

rubrics_metrics.name: NPFM: Director may rule on merits at institution stage / define circumstances where IPR 'shall not be instituted or maintained'
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed rules confirm the Director's role in deciding discretionary denial and further expand that role to also ruling on the merits of the petition at the institution stage, and define specific circumstances where an IPR 'shall not be instituted or maintained.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under this approach the Director could decide both discretionary and merits questions at institution—potentially narrowing opportunities to obtain Board institution on purely merits-based grounds even if discretionary concerns are borderline. Petitioners should prepare stronger institution-stage merits showings and anticipate Director-level merits scrutiny.
